title: Base Camp One: the first full round
summary: Three weeks of separate pieces join into one whole round against a parent, with a young timekeeper on the bell, and then they run the Sprout's card themselves.
materials: the sand timers, two minute and one minute, and the call bell
a parent with opinions and twenty minutes
your flow sheet, a page ruled into columns
a phone for the 90 second speeches
this week's Sprout parent card, paper, crayons and scissors, for the teach-someone-younger quest

steps.title: The whole shape, end to end, and your timekeeper
steps.body:
So far you have held the pieces one at a time: what a round is and what a judge writes on a ballot, then the constructive with its signposts and an evidence slot in every point, then the flow sheet and the rebuttal that answers what was actually said. Today the pieces become one thing.

The shape, three rounds. Round one, constructives, two minutes each, you first: two points, each with a reason and one piece of evidence, signposted so a listener always knows where you are. Round two, rebuttals, 90 seconds each, flow sheet open in front of you: answer their columns, not your notes. The steelman rule stands, and it is strictest here: say their point back so fairly that they nod before you answer it. Round three, closings, one minute each, no new arguments allowed. In a closing you choose, you do not add.

The motion: making a thing yourself is better than buying it. Pick the side you actually lean toward and let the parent take the other one. If you both lean the same way, the parent argues the far side anyway, and watching a grown-up argue against their own belief is a skill worth stealing.

Now your timekeeper: a younger sibling, cousin or friend, or a parent playing the part, too young to read a clock, which is fine, because they do not need to. Train them in two minutes before anyone sits down: you turn the timer, they watch the sand, and when the last grain lands they ring the bell one time. Practise twice with them, and let them ring it both times, because a bell you have never rung is a bell you will ring at the wrong moment. The two minute timer covers the constructives and the one minute timer covers the closings; for the 90 second rebuttals a grown-up runs a phone and nods to them, and the bell is still theirs.

One thing to say out loud to them, and to yourself: the bell is not an interruption and it is not a punishment. It is the referee you and your opponent share, and finishing on time is a skill, not a telling off. When it rings you finish the sentence you are in and stop. If they ring early, laugh, thank them, and keep going. They are young, and they are not the enemy of your speech.

steps.title: Teach someone younger
steps.body:
They timed your round. Now you run theirs.

A parent card is the short card in the app that a grown-up normally does with Sprout. This week it is yours to run, and this one is a story you draw and then cut up: five birds on a branch, and two of them fly away.

Read the card all the way through before you start, so you know where it lands. Then set out paper and crayons and do it with them, not for them. They pick the colours, they draw the birds, they fly them off the page with their own hand. Scissors are the one part a grown-up should be near, so ask one to sit with you for the cutting.

The question is the whole point, and it is easy to forget in the fun: every time some birds fly away, ask how many are left, and then wait. Let them touch each bird as they count, even when it is slow, even when you already know. Waiting is the job.

Watch for one thing that surprises you: a number they land on without counting, or a story they tell back with more in it than you put there.
checklist: I read the card all the way through before I started
They drew the birds and flew them away themselves
I asked how many are left every single time, and waited for them to count
A grown-up was beside us for the scissors
I noticed one thing they did that surprised me

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record round three: both closings, whole face in frame, and the bell at the end if the camera can catch it. Then keep rolling for one honest sentence: which of your opponent's arguments was the strongest, and what would you say to it with another week to think?
